courseTitle: Addressing Problems of Learning through Pedagogy & Technology
headerTitle: EDU654 — Addressing Problems of Learning through Pedagogy & Technology
subtitle: Midterm Important Subjective Questions (Solved)

subjective.question: What is pedagogy? How do pedagogy and technology together address the problems of learning?
subjective.answer: Pedagogy is the art of teaching. When a teacher thinks about the method to teach, that thinking is pedagogy. The problems of learning are the difficulties students face in understanding difficult topics and the difficulties teachers face in communicating those topics properly. Pedagogy provides the methods, strategies and techniques of teaching, while technology provides the tools (media, models, audio, video and digital tools) that enhance instruction. Used together, they help the teacher identify where and what the difficulty in a topic is, design suitable pedagogical content, and make students actually understand the concept instead of only memorizing answers, so that a real change in students' thinking takes place.

subjective.question: What does TPACK stand for? Explain its three knowledge domains and their intersection.
subjective.answer: TPACK stands for Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge. Its three domains are: (1) Content Knowledge - the teacher's knowledge of the subject matter to be taught; (2) Pedagogical Knowledge - knowledge of the methods, processes and practices of teaching and learning; and (3) Technological Knowledge - knowledge of tools and technologies that can be used in teaching. No single domain is sufficient on its own: technological knowledge by itself does not make teaching effective. It is the intersection of content, pedagogical and technological knowledge that provides the guide for effective teaching, because the teacher then knows what to teach, how to teach it, and which technology supports that particular content for the students' level of learning.

subjective.question: What is discovery-based learning? Discuss its main characteristics and the role of the teacher in it.
subjective.answer: Discovery-based learning is a student-centered approach in which students learn by investigating real-life situations and discovering knowledge themselves instead of receiving it ready-made. It is directly linked with the theory of constructivism and it builds on intuition. Its main characteristics are: an emphasis on investigation of real-life situations, students' active involvement in exploring and questioning, learning through experience, and development of understanding rather than rote memorization. The time consumed in discovery learning is worthwhile because the learning is long-lasting. In this approach the teacher's role is that of a facilitator: the teacher presents situations and problems, guides the investigation, asks questions, and helps students reach conclusions themselves - similar to the teacher's role in a discussion - instead of simply presenting concepts.

subjective.question: Differentiate between rote learning and meaningful learning.
subjective.answer: Rote learning is memorizing facts, definitions and answers without understanding them; the knowledge stays at the surface and is soon forgotten. Without reflection, learning is only an activity. Meaningful learning, on the other hand, comes from contradiction, resolution and understanding: the learner connects new knowledge with prior knowledge, understands the logic behind it, and can apply it to solve practical problems. In rote learning only a part of the brain works, while in meaningful learning the understanding and logic levels of the brain are also active, so the student can generate meanings through the concept. A concept taught to students is only meaningful when they understand it and can relate it to their knowledge and real-life situations.

subjective.question: What is reflection? Why is reflection considered an essential part of the learning process?
subjective.answer: Reflection is thinking critically about what has been learned or taught - reviewing it, questioning it and searching it for greater understanding. Reflection is an important part of any learning process: without reflection, learning is only an activity, like watching a show just to pass time. Through reflection, all the learned material can be gathered, sorted and re-sorted, and searched through for deeper understanding and inspiration. Non-intuitive problems also need reflection to be solved. A teacher can reflect on his teaching at the end of the lecture to investigate the level of understanding of the students, and students who reflect convert surface learning into meaningful learning.

subjective.question: Describe the four stages of Polya's method of problem solving.
subjective.answer: George Polya, in his book "How to Solve It", developed a plan to solve the problem which consists of four stages: (1) Understand the problem - the learner should appreciate the problem and be able to identify its inputs and outputs; (2) Devise a plan - make a strategy connecting the data with the unknown; (3) Carry out the plan - execute the strategy step by step; and (4) Look back - examine and reflect on the solution obtained. While posing a problem, the teacher must keep in mind that the learner moves from simple to complex and that the prior knowledge of students is taken into account.

subjective.question: Describe Paul Zeitz's steps of problem solving as given in his book "The Art and Craft of Problem Solving".
subjective.answer: Paul Zeitz, in "The Art and Craft of Problem Solving", compares solving a problem with climbing a mountain and identifies four steps to solve a problem: (1) Strategy level - deciding the overall approach or strategy for attacking the problem; (2) Tactics level - choosing the specific tactics and techniques to implement the strategy; (3) Tools - applying the mathematical tools, techniques and knowledge needed; and (4) Reflection - looking back at the solution, verifying it and learning from the process. Zeitz also emphasizes that problems and exercises are different: an exercise needs only routine application, while a problem needs strategy, tactics and thinking.

subjective.question: What is problem-based learning? Discuss its main features and the classroom environment most conducive to it.
subjective.answer: Problem-based learning is a model of instruction in which learning is organized around problems: the teacher presents situations/problems and students learn by investigating and solving them. Its main features are: authentic investigation, collaboration among students, and production of artifacts; it does NOT have a highly structured learning environment. The classroom environment most conducive for successful problem-based instruction is moderately structured and student centered. When preparing for problem-based instruction, the teacher is concerned with communicating goals clearly, designing interesting and appropriate problem situations and planning logistics - and is least concerned with preparing answers to the problem situation, because students are expected to find the answers themselves.

subjective.question: Define a set. When and where was the concept of sets included in the syllabus?
subjective.answer: A set is any well-defined collection or list of distinct objects. For example, all toys of Ali, all toys of Nariman, and all friends of Ali and Nariman are sets, whereas "multiplication of Ali and Nariman's toys with their friends" is not a set because it is not a well-defined collection of distinct objects. The addition of two sets is found out by applying the union operation. The concept of sets was included for the first time in 1967 in the FSc syllabus.

subjective.question: What is kinematics? Define displacement, velocity and acceleration.
subjective.answer: Kinematics is the branch of mechanics that is concerned with describing the movement of objects; it involves the concepts of displacement, velocity and acceleration. Displacement is the shortest distance between two points (the change in position of an object in a particular direction). Velocity is the rate of change of displacement; the velocity function is a function of time and is the derivative of the position function, giving the velocity of an object at any point in time. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. The average velocity and the instantaneous velocity of an object are the same if the object's acceleration is zero, i.e. the object moves with constant velocity.

subjective.question: What is the Jigsaw method? Discuss its benefits for students.
subjective.answer: The Jigsaw method is a cooperative learning technique in which students work in small groups. Each group member is assigned to become an "expert" on some aspect of a unit of study; experts from different groups meet to discuss their topic, and then return to their groups and teach their topic to their group mates. In the jigsaw technique, students are directly engaged with the material. Its benefits are: students gain depth of understanding instead of having material presented to them; they gain practice in self-teaching, one of the most valuable skills; peer teaching makes them understand the material at a deeper level; they speak the language of the discipline and become fluent in its terminology; every student develops an expertise and has something important to contribute; and the group task promotes discussion, problem-solving, cooperation and active learning.

subjective.question: Differentiate between sustaining and disruptive technology. Why is disruptive technology mostly used by non-consumers?
subjective.answer: Sustaining technology is the established, higher-level technology with which large corporations are designed to work; it improves the performance of established products for existing (mainstream) customers. Disruptive technology is the new technology that unexpectedly displaces an established technology. Existing technology is of a very higher level, whereas disruptive technology is of a lower level which never meets the higher technology. Disruptive technology is mostly popular among non-consumers - the people who could not afford the higher technology - because it is simpler and cheaper; for example, people keenly used transistors because they could not afford expensive technology. There are two categories of new technology: sustaining and disruptive.

subjective.question: Compare the traditional (old) classroom with the modern classroom. What should the future classroom look like?
subjective.answer: In the old classroom there was a single room school with a single instructor, limited content, people from different age groups, many subjects taught at a time, immediate feedback, more discussion method, and teaching on the basis of prior knowledge, with limited technology. In the modern classroom there are many classes in a school, a single instructor for a class, the same content for the whole class, people of the same age groups, one subject taught at a time, no immediate feedback, lecturing, admission after clearing a test, and prior knowledge is not tested - so some students get the topic clearly while others do not, and the focus is on covering the syllabus. The future classroom must consist of the values and methods of the ancient classroom (focus on students' understanding, teaching according to students' interest and needs) combined with modern technology and pedagogy, using content, pedagogy and technology according to students' level of learning.

subjective.question: Why is asking questions important in the classroom? Discuss with reference to the "curious classroom".
subjective.answer: Asking questions is fundamental to learning: asking the right question is fundamental to the process of learning, thinking is driven by questions, and we can stimulate our thinking with questions. In the "curious classroom", carefully crafted questions, generated by both teachers and students, enhance student learning. The psychological state of asking questions in classroom is said to be problem solving, because sometimes even the teacher does not know how to find the answer or how to convey it effectively. A teacher asks questions during a lecture to learn whether students are understanding the lecture or not, to engage and challenge pupils, and to check prior knowledge. Deep questions force us to deal with complexity, while superficial questions produce only superficial understanding. Questions of purpose force us to define our task, and questions define tasks, express problems and delineate issues.

subjective.question: What is metacognition? Why is metacognition not important for rote learning?
subjective.answer: Metacognition is the thinking about the process of thinking - being aware of and regulating one's own thought and learning processes. It is important for problem solving, for assessment of learning and for teaching, because all of these require a learner to monitor, evaluate and improve his own thinking. Metacognition is not important for rote learning because rote learning is mere memorization: the learner simply repeats and stores material without thinking about it, without understanding it, and without monitoring his own learning process, so no thinking about thinking is involved.

subjective.question: Discuss James E. Zull's views on learning and the brain.
subjective.answer: James E. Zull, in his book "The Art of Changing the Brain" (enriching the practice of teaching by exploring the biology of learning), gave the concept of understanding the brain function. According to Zull, learning means changing the brain: when a student learns, physical changes take place in the brain as new connections are made. A better understanding of brain function will promote a more flexible and varied approach to learning, and educators can use knowledge of how the brain works to design better teaching. An effective teacher, therefore, is a continuous learner who teaches in ways that engage the brain's natural learning cycle rather than forcing memorization.

subjective.question: Compare Pakistani and international textbooks for teaching probability, with reference to the use of diagrams.
subjective.answer: While comparing the textbooks used for teaching probability at intermediate level, a clear difference appears in pages and diagrams. The Punjab textbook covers the topic in 13 pages with only 1 diagram; the Sindh Board book covers 19 pages with 4 diagrams; the Baluchistan Board book has 7 pages and no diagram of this concept; the KPK book has 36 pages and 19 diagrams and was far better than the others; India's books have 57 pages and 8 diagrams; the Harvard book has 20 pages and 50 diagrams; and the O Level book has 45 pages and 45 diagrams. The Punjab textbook has numerous theorems, no narration, heavy use of set notation and proofs with heavy notation, and lacks visual tools. The Baluchistan book is full of definitions and formulas with no diagrams, grids or visual tools. The comparison shows that it is vitally essential to provide graphical and visual tools to learners while teaching mathematics, and that Pakistani books rely on rote presentation while international books teach through visualization.

subjective.question: What is thinking? Differentiate between effective and ineffective thinking.
subjective.answer: Thinking is a process of response to external stimuli; it is central to learning, and there is no learning without thinking. Thinking and learning have the same outcomes, so they are very close to each other and cannot be separated; empowering someone as a learner will not happen unless we empower them as thinkers. There are two types of thinking activity: effective and ineffective. Effective thinking is where there is an outcome: it does make changes to world view, belief, opinion, attitude, behaviour, skills, understanding and knowledge. Ineffective thinking doesn't clarify anything, doesn't raise questions, and causes no change or strengthening to world view. Thinking is something abstract, and answers often signal a full step in thought.

subjective.question: What is lateral thinking? Which part of thinking is it concerned with?
subjective.answer: Lateral thinking, a concept associated with Edward de Bono, is thinking for changing concepts and perceptions - moving across patterns in the mind instead of only digging deeper in the same direction, as expressed in the saying, "You cannot dig a hole in a different place by digging the same hole deeper." Lateral thinking is concerned with the perception part of thinking: this is where we organize the world into recognizable pieces and where our assumed perceptions, concepts and boundaries lie. Because the brain is a self-organizing information system, there is a mathematical need for moving across patterns and escaping from a local optimum towards a global optimum; the tools and processes of lateral thinking, such as provocation, are designed to achieve this lateral movement and hence support creativity and problem solving.

subjective.question: What are learning styles? How do kinesthetic learners learn best?
subjective.answer: Learning styles are the preferred ways in which different individuals take in and process information. Learning styles are unique to the individual - they are not unimportant compared to teaching styles and do not simply reveal genetic differences between girls and boys. A teacher should therefore develop pedagogical strategies that allow instant feedback, individual learning pace, and excitement, enjoyment and wonder for students with different styles. Kinesthetic learners, who learn through physical activity and movement, learn best by doing - through hands-on activities, experiments and practice - rather than by hearing lectures or by using text and watching videos in calm, quiet surroundings.

subjective.question: What is Human Computer Interface (HCI)? Discuss the basic HCI heuristics.
subjective.answer: Human Computer Interface (HCI) is the interface through which a user interacts with a computer; while using an HCI, a general purpose computer relies on the front interface to perform an activity. The basic HCI heuristics are: rate of responsiveness (how quickly the system responds), error recognition and communication (the system recognizes errors and communicates them clearly), and interface feedback (the system keeps the user informed about what is happening). Good HCI design is flexible, user friendly and uses fewer system resources; hidden features are not an advantage of learning in HCI. The use of technology to enhance the learning process is called Information Communication Technology (ICT) in education.

subjective.question: Differentiate between behaviorism, cognitivism and constructivism as theories of learning.
subjective.answer: Behaviorism assumes that a learner is essentially passive, responding to environmental stimuli; learning through positive reinforcement (application of a stimulus) and negative reinforcement/punishment are behaviorist techniques, so learning is observed through changes in behavior. Cognitivism goes inside the learner's head: it is the theory of learning associated with mental processes, in which knowledge is viewed as symbolic mental constructs and learning involves how those constructs are committed to memory; logic and deduction are included in the mental process. Constructivism is an educational philosophy which holds that learners ultimately construct their own knowledge by reflecting on their experiences; discovery-based learning has a direct link with constructivism, and constructivist approaches can also be used in online learning through discussion forums, wikis and blogs.

subjective.question: What are learning outcomes? How many levels of learning outcomes are there?
subjective.answer: Learning outcomes are the statements of learning achievements - what a learner is expected to know, understand or be able to do after a learning activity. The degree of success a teacher has in using technology for instruction is mostly dependent on the teacher's ability to achieve these outcomes. Learning outcomes can be measured through examinations or tests to assure the amount of learning that takes place, and a teacher reflects at the end of the lesson to investigate the level of students' understanding. There are three levels of learning outcomes, moving from rote learning at the lowest level, through understanding, to the highest level where the brain's logic works fully and the student can generate meanings through the concept.

subjective.question: Discuss the importance of prior knowledge in learning.
subjective.answer: Prior knowledge is what students already know before new teaching begins, and it is one of the strongest indicators of how well students will learn new information, because prior knowledge helps a person to make sense of the world. New learning is built on existing knowledge schemata, which are the starting point for new learning; therefore it is important to test the prior knowledge of the students before and during teaching. When posing a problem, the teacher must take into account the prior knowledge of students. If prior knowledge (including misconceptions) is ignored, students may memorize answers without understanding - for example, surveys of university students showed that most could not explain basic phenomena like day, night and seasons because their prior misconceptions were never confronted.

subjective.question: What is hypothesis testing? Why do teachers usually avoid it in the classroom, and why should it be promoted?
subjective.answer: Hypothesis testing is the process in which, when a problem is proposed, students visualize it, list down the possible answers (hypotheses), and then think critically on every answer - is it correct, and if yes why, and if not why - and verify the answer logically. Knowledge gained must be linked with hypothesis testing; only then does the students' knowledge base become rich, whereas memorizing answers never makes it rich. Teachers usually avoid hypothesis testing in classroom because it is time consuming, and today the internet can provide answers quickly - but the internet cannot provide hypothesis testing. While hypothesis testing, the best state to learn is creative tension, a situation where disagreement or discord ultimately gives rise to better ideas or outcomes, so teachers must focus more on hypothesis testing instead of recommending internet search.

subjective.question: Discuss the role of visualization and the visual system in learning.
subjective.answer: Images are a very powerful support for thinking, and visualization is one of the most effective techniques for addressing problems of learning. The visual system has a modelling power: it can model concepts in the mind. The human brain can search for more than 50,000 images per second in long term memory, and when information is presented to students through visualization, it is stored in long term memory, which makes learning durable. Problem solving through visualization, the use of diagrams, grids, tables and probability trees, and story-based visualization (as in Khan Academy lectures) help students understand difficult concepts; this is why books with more diagrams teach probability better than books with none. Visualization also supports discovery learning and helps students confront their misconceptions.
